title: Carcinoma Breast: current answers, not old keys
subject: surgery
summary: Diagnose, stage and treat breast cancer the way today's papers ask, and unlearn the old PYQ keys.

objectives.text: Choose the current answers to 'most common' questions (cancer in women, site, type, subtype), rejecting the old cervix key
Tell invasive lobular from ductal carcinoma, and match BRCA1/BRCA2 to chromosome, tumour type and male breast cancer
Pick the triple-assessment components and the right imaging and tissue test for a breast lump, including why core biopsy beats FNAC
Decide who needs staging scans, and name the metastatic site and prognostic factor
Assign the T category from skin, chest-wall and inflammatory findings (peau d'orange, pectoralis, T4d)
Place nodal findings on the N ladder and say when disease is M1 (supraclavicular is N3c)
Choose between Halsted, MRM and breast conservation for an operable cancer, and tell Halsted from MRM
Decide BCS suitability, SLNB versus ALND, and radiotherapy after surgery
Pick the treatment sequence for locally advanced and inflammatory carcinoma
Choose the hormonal agent by menopausal status and predict tamoxifen and AI toxicity, chemoprevention and classic LCIS plan
Name the HER2 drug and its reversible cardiotoxicity, contrasted with doxorubicin
Predict the nerve deficit and complication after axillary dissection or mastectomy

A 58-year-old woman has a thickened area in one breast that does not feel like a clear lump. Biopsy shows small, uniform cells lined up one behind another. Mammography shows no mass.
Which type is this?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ignore which type is commonest. Ask how the cells sit: glands in a firm mass, or one behind another?
That is not the right choice. Ductal is the commonest type, so it feels like the default answer to every type question.
But ductal cancer usually forms one hard, stellate mass, and this biopsy shows a line of cells with no mass. Commonest is not the same as fits the picture.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: a common type is not the answer to a question about spread.

say.text: That is not the right choice. Medullary is a real type, but it does not fit single-file cells.
Medullary is soft and well defined, with a lymphocytic infiltrate, so it forms a clear mass.
Yes. Lobular cells grow in single file because E-cadherin is lost, so they spread through the breast without forming one mass.
That is also why lobular is more often bilateral and multicentric.
Yes. Ductal is the commonest type: a hard, gritty, stellate mass, the scirrhous picture.
Lobular cells lie in single file with loss of E-cadherin. They are often bilateral and multicentric, and spread to peritoneum, ovaries and meninges.
Commonest and bilateral are different questions. Luminal A is the most common molecular subtype.
Years after a breast cancer, a woman has deposits in the peritoneum and ovaries, and a tumour in the other breast.
Which primary type is most likely?
That is not the right choice. The scirrhous ductal mass is the picture most people hold for breast cancer, so it becomes the default.
Spread to the peritoneum and ovaries, with the other breast involved, is the lobular pattern.
That is not the right choice. Medullary is soft and well defined, and it is not known for this pattern of spread.
Medullary carcinoma has a lymphocytic infiltrate and a clear edge, which does not explain peritoneal and ovarian deposits.
Yes. Peritoneal and ovarian deposits with a bilateral picture are the lobular pattern.
BRCA1 and BRCA2 are two separate breast cancer genes, each on its own chromosome arm.
Which pairing of gene and arm is right?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Each gene has its own arm. Do not learn the two numbers as one unordered pair.
That is not the right choice. The numbers 13 and 17 come as a pair, so it is easy to swap which gene owns which.
The exam tests the gene-to-arm link, so each gene needs its own fact.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the swap: the pair of numbers is not the fact to remember.

say.text: Yes. BRCA1 is on 17q and BRCA2 on 13q.
A breast and ovarian cancer family has a mutation on chromosome 17q.
Which gene is it?
That is not the right choice. Two numbers that go together are easy to swap, so 17q slides to the wrong gene.
Here the arm is the clue: attach each arm to its own gene, not to a number pair.
Yes. BRCA1 is on 17q, so a 17q mutation in a breast and ovarian family points to BRCA1.
Male breast cancer is rare. Which gene is it most linked to?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the phenotype before the famous gene: male breast cancer is not the triple-negative pattern.

say.text: That is not the right choice. PTEN is a real cancer gene, but it belongs to a different hereditary syndrome.

Yes. BRCA2 is the gene more tied to male breast cancer, along with Klinefelter syndrome.
BRCA1 cancers are typically triple-negative, the basal-like pattern.

Which pairing is most likely?
That is not the right choice. BRCA1 is the gene you reach for first, so it tempts you to label both families with it.

That is not the right choice. BRCA2 fits family B, the man, but not family A.
Triple-negative cancers in several women are the BRCA1 pattern, so one gene for both families cannot work.
Yes. Triple-negative cancers in women fit BRCA1, and breast cancer in a man fits BRCA2.

choices.label: Inflamed skin, so it means inflammatory carcinoma
Blocked subdermal lymphatics, so the skin swells
Cooper's ligaments pulling the skin inward
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice. Any skin change over a lump can tempt you to read it as the inflammatory syndrome.

That is not the right choice. Dimpling is a real skin sign, but it has a different cause from orange-peel oedema.

Ductal and lobular cancer look and spread differently.
Which pairing is right?

choices.label: Ductal: one hard stellate mass; lobular: single-file cells, E-cadherin lost
Ductal: single-file cells; lobular: one hard stellate mass
Both form one hard mass; ductal is just the commoner
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about how each type lays its cells down, and which one is known for E-cadherin loss.
That is not the right choice. The two pictures are swapped.
The hard, gritty, stellate mass is ductal. Single-file cells with E-cadherin loss are lobular.
That is not the right choice. Ductal is the commonest, so it is easy to let lobular borrow its picture.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that commonest does not mean the same behaviour.

say.text: That is not the right choice. This pairing is reversed.

A 35-year-old woman comes to you with bloody discharge from one duct of the breast. Nothing is palpable.
Predict first: what is the most common cause?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Intraductal papilloma is the commonest cause of bloody discharge from a single duct.
Carcinoma still has to be excluded. Retraction, bloody discharge and eczema-like change are the nipple signs that need a work-up.
That is not the right choice: bloody discharge is the alarming sign, so carcinoma feels like the commonest cause.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read the qualifier in the stem: 'most common' asks how often, not how worrying.

choices.label: T4b, skin involvement by the tumour
T3, because the tumour is large
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A red, warm, swollen breast with peau d'orange over at least one-third of it is T4d, often with no discrete lump.

That choice is not right: peau d'orange does put a tumour in T4b, so the sign feels like the answer.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the sign from the picture: peau d'orange alone is T4b, the red warm swollen breast is T4d.

say.text: Ask whether this is one patch of skin over a tumour, or the whole breast looking inflamed.

choices.label: Ultrasound for the 28-year-old, mammography for the 52-year-old

Not sure, give me a hint

choices.label: Fine needle aspiration cytology of the breast area
Stereotactic-guided core needle biopsy of the area
Not sure, give me a hint

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the pathologist must report before you name the sample.

Whole-body bone scan to exclude distant spread first
Not sure, give me a hint

K1.text: Breast cancer is the **most common cancer in women** in India and worldwide.

K3.text: **Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type (NST)** is the most common histological type, forming about 70–80% of cases.

K4.text: **BRCA1** lies on chromosome **17q** and **BRCA2** on chromosome **13q**; BRCA2 is the one more associated with **male** breast cancer.

K5.text: **Triple assessment** = clinical examination + imaging (mammography and/or ultrasound) + tissue diagnosis (**core needle biopsy** preferred over FNAC).

K6.text: **Axillary lymph node status** is the single most important prognostic factor.

K7.text: **Peau d'orange** is caused by obstruction of the subdermal (cutaneous) lymphatics with skin oedema, and puts the tumour in **T4b**.

K8.text: **Inflammatory carcinoma (T4d)** is due to tumour emboli in dermal lymphatics, and is treated with **neoadjuvant chemotherapy → modified radical mastectomy → radiotherapy**, never breast-conserving surgery.

K9.text: **Ipsilateral supraclavicular** node involvement is **N3c**, not M1, in current AJCC staging.

K10.text: **Tamoxifen** is the hormonal agent for ER-positive **premenopausal** women; **aromatase inhibitors** (letrozole, anastrozole, exemestane) are preferred in **postmenopausal** women.

K11.text: **Trastuzumab** targets HER2 and its key toxicity is **cardiotoxicity** (usually reversible, not dose-dependent).

K12.text: The **intercostobrachial nerve** is the nerve most often injured/sacrificed in axillary dissection, giving numbness of the medial upper arm; injury to the **long thoracic nerve** gives **winging of the scapula**.

K16.text: Hereditary syndromes: **BRCA1** and **BRCA2** mutations, **Li-Fraumeni** syndrome (**TP53**), **Cowden** syndrome (**PTEN**), **Peutz-Jeghers** syndrome (**STK11**), ataxia-telangiectasia (**ATM**), and hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (**CDH1**, linked to lobular carcinoma).

K22.text: **Klinefelter syndrome** and BRCA2 mutation are risk factors for **male breast cancer**, which forms about **1%** of all breast cancers.

K25.text: **LCIS**: often bilateral and multicentric, does not form a lump or calcify, and is a **risk marker** for invasive cancer in either breast.

K26.text: **Invasive ductal carcinoma (NST)**: the most common type; forms a hard, gritty, stellate mass (**scirrhous** carcinoma).

K27.text: **Invasive lobular carcinoma**: cells in single file (**"Indian file"**) due to loss of **E-cadherin**; more often **bilateral and multicentric**, and spreads unusually to **peritoneum, GI tract, ovaries and meninges**.

K28.text: **Medullary carcinoma**: soft, well-circumscribed, with a prominent **lymphocytic infiltrate**, associated with BRCA1 and triple-negative status.

K32.text: Luminal A — ER+ and/or PR+, HER2−, low Ki-67

K39.text: Local spread is along ducts and fascial planes; involvement of **Cooper's (suspensory) ligaments** causes **skin dimpling**, and ductal involvement/fibrosis causes **nipple retraction**.

K42.text: **Bone** is the most common site of distant metastasis, mostly **osteolytic**; lung, liver and brain are other common sites.

K43.text: Most commonly a **painless, hard, irregular lump** with ill-defined margins.

K45.text: Nipple signs: **recent retraction**, **bloody discharge**, and eczema-like change (Paget's).

K46.text: In Paget's disease the change **starts at the nipple and spreads to the areola**, whereas eczema starts on the areola, is often bilateral and itchy, and spares the nipple.

K47.text: **Fixity to pectoralis major** is tested by examining with the muscle contracted (hands pressed on hips).

K48.text: **Inflammatory carcinoma** presents as a red, warm, swollen breast with peau d'orange involving at least **one-third** of the breast, often without a discrete lump, mimicking mastitis.

K49.text: **Mammography** is the screening tool of choice and the main imaging test in women over about 35–40 years.

K50.text: Mammographic signs of malignancy are a **spiculated (stellate) mass** and **clustered pleomorphic microcalcifications**.

K51.text: **Ultrasound** is preferred in women **under 35** and in dense breasts, and distinguishes solid from cystic lesions.

K52.text: **MRI** is the most sensitive imaging test; it is used for **screening high-risk women (e.g. BRCA carriers)**, assessing **silicone implants**, judging extent of **lobular** carcinoma, and finding the primary in **occult breast cancer** presenting with axillary nodes.

K54.text: **Core needle (trucut) biopsy** is the preferred tissue test because it distinguishes invasive from in situ cancer and gives grade and **ER/PR/HER2** status.

K55.text: **Stereotactic or ultrasound-guided** biopsy is used for impalpable lesions such as microcalcifications.

K56.text: FNAC is used mainly for **axillary nodes** and cysts.

K57.text: Routine metastatic work-up is not needed in early asymptomatic disease; it (CT chest/abdomen, bone scan, or PET-CT) is done for locally advanced disease or symptoms.

K58.text: **CA 15-3** and **CEA** are used for monitoring metastatic disease, not for screening or diagnosis.

K64.text: T4a — Extension to **chest wall** (ribs, intercostal muscles, serratus anterior; **not pectoralis muscle alone**)

K65.text: T4b — **Skin**: ulceration, ipsilateral satellite nodules, or **peau d'orange**

K74.text: M1 — Distant metastasis (including contralateral axillary/supraclavicular nodes)

K75.text: **Locally advanced breast cancer (LABC)** means stage III disease: tumours > 5 cm with nodes, T4 tumours, or N2/N3 nodal disease.

K76.text: Early breast cancer is treated with **surgery to the breast and axilla**, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy and systemic therapy as indicated by stage and receptor status.

K77.text: **Breast-conserving surgery (BCS)** (wide local excision with clear margins) plus **whole-breast radiotherapy** gives survival **equivalent** to mastectomy in suitable early cancers.

K78.text: For invasive cancer treated with BCS, an adequate margin is **"no ink on tumour"**.

K79.text: **Multicentric disease** (tumours in separate quadrants) or **diffuse malignant-appearing microcalcifications**.

K80.text: **Previous radiotherapy** to the breast or chest wall.

K81.text: **Pregnancy** when radiotherapy would be needed during pregnancy.

K84.text: Relative: a **large tumour relative to breast size** (poor cosmesis) and active **connective tissue disease** (scleroderma, SLE) that increases radiation toxicity.

K85.text: **Halsted radical mastectomy** removes the breast, **pectoralis major and minor**, and all three axillary levels; it is now rarely done.

K86.text: **Modified radical mastectomy (MRM)** removes the breast and axillary nodes while preserving **pectoralis major**.

K89.text: **Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB)** is the standard axillary staging for **clinically node-negative** invasive cancer, using **radioisotope (Tc-99m sulphur colloid)** and/or **blue dye** (isosulfan blue / methylene blue).

K90.text: SLNB is **contraindicated** in **inflammatory breast cancer** and in **biopsy-proven node-positive** axilla, where axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) is done.

K91.text: After the **ACOSOG Z0011** trial, women with **1–2 positive sentinel nodes** treated with BCS and whole-breast radiotherapy can **omit ALND**.

K95.text: **Neoadjuvant chemotherapy** is used for **LABC** and **inflammatory** cancer, and to downstage operable tumours to allow BCS.

K97.text: **Tamoxifen** (a SERM) for **5–10 years** is used for hormone-receptor-positive **premenopausal** women.

K98.text: **Aromatase inhibitors** are preferred for hormone-receptor-positive **postmenopausal** women, because postmenopausal oestrogen comes from peripheral aromatisation.

K99.text: Tamoxifen side effects: **endometrial carcinoma**, **thromboembolism (DVT/PE)**, hot flushes and **cataract**.

K101.text: **Trastuzumab** (anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody) is given for **1 year** in HER2-positive disease; its cardiotoxicity is usually **reversible and not dose-related**, unlike the **dose-dependent** cardiomyopathy of **anthracyclines (doxorubicin)**.

K103.text: **DCIS**: treated with **BCS + radiotherapy** or **mastectomy**; routine ALND is not done, and **SLNB is done if mastectomy** is performed.

K104.text: **Classic LCIS**: managed with **surveillance** and consideration of **chemoprevention**, not mastectomy.

K110.text: **Chemoprevention** uses **tamoxifen**, **raloxifene** (postmenopausal; no increase in endometrial cancer) or aromatase inhibitors.

K112.text: Of axillary dissection: **lymphoedema of the arm**, seroma, shoulder stiffness, and nerve injury.

K113.text: **Intercostobrachial nerve** injury → numbness of the medial upper arm/axilla.

K114.text: **Long thoracic nerve (of Bell)** injury → paralysis of **serratus anterior** → **winging of the scapula**.

K118.text: Most common cancer in women (India and world) — Breast cancer

K119.text: Most common site in breast — Upper outer quadrant

K120.text: Most common histological type — Invasive ductal carcinoma, NST

K122.text: Type most often bilateral/multicentric — Invasive lobular carcinoma

K123.text: Most common site of distant metastasis — Bone

K124.text: Most important prognostic factor — Axillary lymph node status

K125.text: Most common molecular subtype — Luminal A

K127.text: Imaging of choice in women < 35 yrs — Ultrasound

K129.text: Investigation of choice for tissue diagnosis — Core needle biopsy

K130.text: Axillary staging in clinically node-negative disease — Sentinel lymph node biopsy

K131.text: Hormonal drug of choice, ER+ premenopausal — Tamoxifen

K132.text: Hormonal drug of choice, ER+ postmenopausal — Aromatase inhibitor (letrozole/anastrozole)

K134.text: Nerve most commonly injured in ALND — Intercostobrachial nerve

K136.text: PYQs have expected **carcinoma cervix** as the most common cancer in Indian women; breast cancer has since overtaken it and is now the most common.

K137.text: PYQs have expected **FNAC** as the investigation of choice for a breast lump; current practice is **core needle biopsy**, which gives histology and receptor status.

K138.text: Older classifications and PYQs counted **supraclavicular nodes** as **M1**; current AJCC staging places them in **N3c**.

K139.text: Older keys gave **radical (Halsted) mastectomy** for operable cancer; current practice is **BCS + radiotherapy** or **MRM**.

K140.text: Exam trap: **peau d'orange** is **T4b**, not T4d; **T4d** needs the clinical picture of inflammatory carcinoma.

K141.text: Exam trap: invasion of **pectoralis major alone** is **not T4a** chest-wall involvement.

K143.text: Exam trap: **tamoxifen** raises the risk of endometrial cancer, but **raloxifene** does not.

cards.q: Which breast cancer type is more often bilateral and multicentric?
cards.a: Invasive lobular carcinoma, with single-file cells and E-cadherin loss.

cards.q: Which BRCA gene is linked to male breast cancer, and which to triple-negative tumours?
cards.a: BRCA2 for male breast cancer; BRCA1 for triple-negative.

cards.q: What causes peau d'orange over a tumour?
cards.a: Blocked subdermal lymphatics causing skin oedema; Cooper's ligament pull gives dimpling.

cards.q: Which tissue test for a breast lump, and why not FNAC?
cards.a: Core needle biopsy, the investigation of choice; FNAC is the old key. Under 35, ultrasound is the imaging.

cards.q: When are distant-spread scans done in breast cancer?
cards.a: For locally advanced disease or symptoms, not routinely in early asymptomatic cancer. Bone is the commonest distant site.

cards.q: Which operation for operable breast cancer, and how do Halsted and MRM differ?
cards.a: Breast conservation with radiotherapy when suitable, or MRM. Halsted removes pectoralis major and minor; MRM keeps pectoralis major.

cards.q: First axillary step for a clinically node-negative patient?
cards.a: Sentinel lymph node biopsy; clear the axilla if the sentinel node is positive.

cards.q: First treatment for stage III or inflammatory breast cancer?
cards.a: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy to downstage, then surgery, then radiotherapy.

cards.q: Hormone drug by menopausal status, and tamoxifen's endometrial effect?
cards.a: Tamoxifen premenopausal; aromatase inhibitor postmenopausal. Tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk.

cards.q: Which nerve is most often injured in axillary clearance, and what does long thoracic injury cause?
cards.a: Intercostobrachial, giving numbness of the medial arm; long thoracic injury gives winging of the scapula.
